body.statement:
The asserted whole-array uniform selector-conditional convergence is false under \(\mathcal M(D_{\mathrm{gap}})\) as defined.  More precisely, for admissible fixed positive margins there is, for every sufficiently large integer \(q\), a whole triangular array \((P_j^{(q)})_{j\geq1}\in\mathcal M(0)\) such that \(\operatorname{Var}(D)=39/625\), \(V_s^{\mathrm{gap}}=V_s=1\) for every \(s\in\mathcal S\), and the stacked limiting covariance is singular, but, with
\[
T_q=\frac{\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{gap}}-\tau}{\widehat{\operatorname{se}}_{\widehat J_A}},
\]
one has
\[
\liminf_{q\to\infty}
\mathbb E_{P_q^{(q)}}\!\left[
 \sup_{x\in\mathbb R}
 \left|\Pr_{P_q^{(q)}}\{T_q\leq x\mid\mathcal F_A\}-\Phi(x)\right|
\right]\geq\frac12.
\]
Thus positive limiting marginal variances and coordinatewise studentization do not compensate for the absence of a uniform finite-row variance and distributional-stabilization condition.
body.proof_tex:
We construct an explicit diagonal witness.  Set the post-period length in row \(j\) equal to \(m_j=j\), so the sample-ratio assumption holds with \(r=1\).  Fix \(\kappa=1/4\), \(\nu=1/100\), arbitrary positive geometric-mixing constants, and a moment envelope larger than the finite primitive moment calculated below.  Since the construction is independent over time, its absolute-regularity coefficients are zero and hence satisfy the declared geometric beta-mixing assumption for those constants.

For each sufficiently large integer \(q\), define a whole array \((P_j^{(q)})_{j\geq1}\).  In every row let the observations be independent and identically distributed over \(t\).  Let \((U_t,E_t,F_t)\) be centered Gaussian with
\[
\operatorname{Var}(U_t)=\operatorname{Var}(E_t)=\operatorname{Var}(F_t)=1,
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(E_t,F_t)=\frac12,
\]
and let \(U_t\) be independent of \((E_t,F_t)\).  Put
\[
Y_t(0)=U_t,qquad
A_t=(U_t+E_t,E_t)^{\prime},qquad
B_t=(U_t+F_t,F_t)^{\prime}.
\]
The controls comprise the four coordinates in \((A_t^{\prime},B_t^{\prime})^{\prime}\).  Role \(1\) uses donor vector \(A_t\) and proxy vector \(B_t\), whereas role \(2\) uses donor vector \(B_t\) and proxy vector \(A_t\).  These are two predeclared, disjoint, square donor/proxy assignments.

Let \(I_t\) be Bernoulli with success probability \(p_q=q^{-2}\), let \(\xi_t\sim N(0,1)\), and make \((I_t,\xi_t)\) independent of all controls.  The treatment-effect coordinate in row \(j\) is
\[
\Delta_t=
\begin{cases}
I_t-p_q+\epsilon_q\xi_t,&j=q,\\
\xi_t,&j\neq q,
\end{cases}
\qquad \epsilon_q=q^{-3}.
\]
Thus \(\mathbb E_{P_j^{(q)}}[\Delta_t]=0\) in every row, so the causal target fixed by the definition of \(\tau\) is \(\tau=0\).  In post-treatment periods the observed treated outcome is \(Y_t(0)+\Delta_t\), exactly as required by the sampling setup.

Strict stationarity holds in every row because each row is independent and identically distributed over the two-sided time index.  Moreover, for every fixed \(\delta_0>0\), Gaussian moment finiteness, \(0\leq I_t\leq1\), and \(0<\epsilon_q\leq1\) give
\[
\sup_{q\geq1}\sup_{j\geq1}
\mathbb E_{P_j^{(q)}}\lVert X_t\rVert^{8+\delta_0}<\infty.
\]
Choosing \(C_{\mathrm{mom}}\) at least this finite number verifies the declared moment-bound assumption.

We next verify bridge rank and bridge centering rather than assuming them.  For \(e=(1,-1)^{\prime}\), one has the pointwise identities
\[
A_t^{\prime}e=B_t^{\prime}e=U_t=Y_t(0).
\]
For both roles the bridge moment matrix is the symmetric matrix
\[
M_1=\mathbb E[B_tA_t^{\prime}]
=M_2=\mathbb E[A_tB_t^{\prime}]
=
\begin{pmatrix}
3/2&1/2\\
1/2&1/2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its eigenvalues are \(1\pm2^{-1/2}\), so
\[
\sigma_{\min}(M_s)=1-2^{-1/2}>\frac14=\kappa.
\]
Also \(M_se=\mathbb E[Z_{s,t}Y_t(0)]\).  Invertibility and the definition of \(\alpha_s\) therefore imply \(\alpha_s=e\), and hence
\[
Y_t(0)-W_{D_s,t}^{\prime}\alpha_s=0
\quad\text{almost surely},
\qquad s\in\mathcal S.
\]
This proves the bridge-centering condition.  Since \(\mu_s=0\), the definition \(H_s=-\mu_s^{\prime}M_s^{-1}\) also gives \(H_s=0\), whence \(u_{s,t}=0\), \(\psi_{s,t}=0\), and \(A_s=0\) for both roles.

The two ridge populations have the same donor covariance and cross moment,
\[
\Sigma=\mathbb E[A_tA_t^{\prime}]=\mathbb E[B_tB_t^{\prime}]
=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
b=\mathbb E[A_tU_t]=\mathbb E[B_tU_t]
=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Thus, by the definitions of \(K_s\) and \(a_s\),
\[
K_s=I_2+\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
a_s=K_s^{-1}b=\begin{pmatrix}2/5\\-1/5\end{pmatrix}.
\]
It follows directly from the definition of \(\ell_{s,t}\) that
\[
\ell_{1,t}=\frac{(3U_t-E_t)^2}{25}+\frac15,
\qquad
\ell_{2,t}=\frac{(3U_t-F_t)^2}{25}+\frac15,
\]
and therefore \(L_1=L_2=3/5\) in every row.  Hence
\[
\sup_{j\geq1}\left|\sqrt j(L_{1,j}-L_{2,j})\right|=0,
\]
which verifies the bounded-selector-gap assumption with \(D_{\mathrm{gap}}=0\), and also with any larger fixed envelope.

The centered one-period loss contrast is
\[
\ell_{1,t}-\ell_{2,t}
=\frac{(F_t-E_t)(6U_t-E_t-F_t)}{25}.
\]
The two factors on the right are jointly Gaussian and centered.  Their covariance is zero, while their variances are respectively \(1\) and \(39\); hence they are independent and
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\ell_{1,t}-\ell_{2,t})=\frac{39}{625}.
\]
For completeness, Gaussianity of every required normalized sum follows directly by a characteristic-function expansion.  If \(Z_t\) denotes the centered six-coordinate score vector in any regular row \(j>q\) and \(\Sigma_Z=\operatorname{Var}(Z_t)\), then \(\mathbb E\lVert Z_t\rVert^3<\infty\), and for each fixed vector \(c\),
\[
\mathbb E\exp\!\left\{\frac{\mathrm i c^{\prime}Z_t}{\sqrt j}\right\}
=1-\frac{c^{\prime}\Sigma_Zc}{2j}+O(j^{-3/2}).
\]
Independence over \(t\) gives
\[
\left(1-\frac{c^{\prime}\Sigma_Zc}{2j}+O(j^{-3/2})\right)^j
\longrightarrow \exp\!\left(-\frac12c^{\prime}\Sigma_Zc\right).
\]
Thus the covariance-limit assumption holds and the Gaussian selector coordinate satisfies \(\operatorname{Var}(D)=39/625>\nu\).

For all rows \(j>q\), the exact bridge residual implies \(v_{1,t}=v_{2,t}=\Delta_t=\xi_t\).  Consequently
\[
V_s=\operatorname{Var}(A_s)+r\operatorname{Var}(R_s)=0+1=1>\nu.
\]
The variance-inheritance lemma gives \(V_s^{\mathrm{gap}}=1\), because \(\operatorname{Var}(A_s)=0\).  The limiting stacked covariance is nevertheless singular: both pre-ATT coordinates vanish and the two post-ATT coordinates coincide.  Since, for a fixed \(q\), every row after row \(q\) has this same regular law, the single exceptional row cannot alter any covariance limit.  We have now verified every member condition in the definition of \(\mathcal M(0)\), so \((P_j^{(q)})_{j\geq1}\in\mathcal M(0)\).

It remains to calculate the failure at the exceptional row.  On the late fitting block, the sample bridge equation for role \(1\) has right-hand side
\[
|\mathcal B_q|^{-1}\sum_{t\in\mathcal B_q}B_tY_t(0)
=\left\{|\mathcal B_q|^{-1}\sum_{t\in\mathcal B_q}B_tA_t^{\prime}\right\}e,
\]
and the analogous identity holds for role \(2\).  The displayed random square matrices are invertible almost surely once \(|\mathcal B_q|\geq2\): their determinants are nonzero polynomials of a continuously distributed Gaussian sample and are not identically zero.  Thus the late bridge estimate equals \(e\) exactly for either selected role.  By the construction of the gap-split estimator,
\[
\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{gap}}
=\frac1q\sum_{t=q+1}^{2q}\Delta_t.
\]
The fitted pre-score is identically zero, and the two roles have the same fitted post residual.  The Bartlett standard error is therefore the same for both roles.  It is strictly positive almost surely because \(\epsilon_q>0\), the centered Gaussian perturbation is nonzero almost surely, and the finite Bartlett kernel matrix is positive definite.  Hence the sign of \(T_q\) is the sign of the post-period sample mean, regardless of which \(\mathcal F_A\)-measurable role is selected.

Independence over time makes the post block independent of \(\mathcal F_A\).  Therefore, almost surely,
\[
\Pr_{P_q^{(q)}}\{T_q\leq0\mid\mathcal F_A\}
=\Pr\!\left\{\frac1q\sum_{t=q+1}^{2q}\Delta_t\leq0\right\}.
\]
On the event that every post-period Bernoulli variable is zero, the post mean equals \(-p_q+\epsilon_q\overline\xi_q\), where \(\sqrt q\,\overline\xi_q\sim N(0,1)\).  Consequently
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr_{P_q^{(q)}}\{T_q\leq0\mid\mathcal F_A\}
&\geq (1-p_q)^q
\Pr\{\epsilon_q\overline\xi_q\leq p_q\}\\
&=(1-q^{-2})^q\Phi\!\left(\frac{p_q\sqrt q}{\epsilon_q}\right)\\
&=(1-q^{-2})^q\Phi(q^{3/2})\longrightarrow1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(\Phi(0)=1/2\), evaluation of the Kolmogorov supremum at \(x=0\) yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E_{P_q^{(q)}}\!\left[
\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}
\left|\Pr_{P_q^{(q)}}\{T_q\leq x\mid\mathcal F_A\}-\Phi(x)\right|
\right]\\
&\qquad\geq
\left|\Pr_{P_q^{(q)}}\{T_q\leq0\mid\mathcal F_A\}-\frac12\right|
\longrightarrow\frac12.
\end{aligned}
\]
For each \(q\), the array just constructed is one of the arrays over which the row-\(q\) supremum is taken.  The supremum is therefore bounded below by this diagonal sequence, proving the stated lower bound and the negative answer.  The obstruction is not singular Gaussian mapping: it is that pointwise covariance convergence and limiting variance margins impose no uniform restriction on the row at which the supremum is evaluated.
body.justification: The diagonal counterexample identifies the exact quantifier failure in the proposed uniform guarantee.
body.gap: Pointwise covariance limits and limiting variance margins do not control the evaluation row uniformly over whole triangular arrays.
body.consumer: Any valid split-sample redesign must strengthen the class with uniform rowwise stabilization before claiming uniform selector-conditional inference.
